# Cinematography grammar

How shots join into one film rather than a row of clips. Use it to plan the
[breakdown](breakdown.md)'s camera language and the [shot list](shot-list.md),
and when writing each shot's prompt in generation. It distils Daniel Arijon's
*Grammar of the Film Language* and Walter Murch's *In the Blink of an Eye*.

Every item here is a default, with the reason it works and when breaking it
works better. None of it is a rule to enforce.

## What wins

1. **The user's vision.** A style the user asks for (handheld jump cuts, a
   locked-off camera that never cuts in, crossing the line on every reverse,
   one unbroken take) replaces the defaults it touches. Record it in the
   breakdown's camera language, follow it in every shot, and never "fix" it.
2. **Emotion, then story, then rhythm.** Murch ranks a cut by whether it is
   true to the emotion of the moment, advances the story and lands on the
   rhythm, ahead of where the eye is looking, screen direction and the room's
   geography. An emotionally right cut hides a small spatial slip; a spatially
   perfect cut that feels wrong is still wrong.
3. **Spatial grammar** (below): what keeps the viewer oriented.

A shot that breaks a default on purpose says so in its `ruleBreak` ("crosses
the line: she has lost control of the room"). That note is for the plan, not a
problem to resolve.

## Cut in pairs

A cut makes sense when the second shot answers the first. End a shot
mid-action or on a look, and open the next on the result or on what was seen.
Plan most cuts as a pair, and write the pair into both shots' Why:

- **Action, then result:** she throws the glass; it shatters against the door.
- **Look, then what is seen:** his eyes go to the window; the car is outside
  ([match eyelines](#joining-shots-inside-a-scene)).
- **Cause, then reaction:** the knock; she freezes.
- **Wide, medium, close:** inside a scene, step in as it climbs, each shot
  showing closer what the one before set up (approach and recede, below).

Two shots in a row against the same background read as one shot jumping,
unless they continue one another; change the angle onto a different part of
the set. In a narrative film, a shot that answers nothing and sets up nothing
has no place in the cut. *Break it* in a montage, whose shots join by rhythm and a constant element
instead.

## Joining shots inside a scene

- **Start and end in motion.** Cut while something is still moving, or a few
  frames after a movement settles. The incoming shot opens on its own action
  already under way (another action, a look, a reaction), not the same motion
  picked up from the other side of the cut, which is match on action (below),
  made only by choice. Movement at the cut softens the change in size or
  angle. A shot
  that eases in from stillness and holds still at its end makes every cut land
  on a dead frame, which is what makes a film feel segmented. *Break it* for a
  held stillness that is the point: a reaction, a tableau, an ending.
- **Match on action, only by choice.** Carrying one action across the cut (a
  hand lifts the letter in the wide, the lift completes in the close-up) is a
  tool for a moment the story turns on, not the way shots join. In generated
  video it needs two separate generations to repeat one motion at the same
  speed, and they rarely do: the action doubles or the pose pops at the cut. Use
  it only where the user asks for it or the story needs that exact moment seen
  twice, and check the cut at normal speed. The default is a plain cut on a
  completed action, a look or a reaction.
- **Keep screen direction.** Draw the line between the two players, or along a
  subject's path, and keep the camera on one side: A stays frame left, B frame
  right, a walk left to right stays left to right. *To cross it smoothly:* cut
  away and back, pass through a neutral shot head-on or tail-away, move the
  camera across the line on screen, or let a character turn and lead the
  camera. *Break it* to disorient or to mark a shift of power; Ozu crossed it
  as a consistent style.
- **Match eyelines.** Two people talking look in opposite directions; both
  looking the same way reads as both looking at a third thing. An off-screen
  look in one shot is answered by what is looked at in the next (the Kuleshov
  pairing: a neutral face takes the meaning of what it looks at).
- **Change enough.** Between two shots of the same subject, change the angle
  by about 30° or more, or the size clearly. A smaller change reads as an
  error. *Break it* as a jump cut: three cuts pushing in on one axis for
  emphasis, or jumps from a fixed camera to compress time.
- **Enter and exit.** Cut as a subject clears the frame and bring them into
  the next from the opposite side. An exit and entry also makes two places feel
  adjacent.
- **Approach and recede.** Open wide enough to place people, move closer as
  the scene climbs to its peak, pull back to rest, and re-establish once
  mid-scene so the viewer keeps the geography. *Break it* by opening on a
  detail and revealing the place later.
- **Motivate every move.** A move has a reason (follow, reveal, approach) and
  a settled start and end (of the whole run, when CONTINUE joins its
  segments); one move per shot or run. A cut is faster than a pan that
  shows nothing on the way. *Break it* with restless handheld when that is the
  film's voice. A [travelling long take](#long-takes) is still one move: a
  continuous path whose position and framing change at waypoints.
- **Let the listener carry it.** A reaction is often stronger than the line.
  Cut to the listener mid-line while the voice continues (an L-cut), or bring
  the next voice in before its face (a J-cut). Cuts exactly on line boundaries
  feel mechanical.

## Joining scenes

A plain cut is the default between scenes, and it needs no link. A film feels
like a slideshow when its clips ease in from a standstill and freeze at their
end ([start and end in motion](#joining-shots-inside-a-scene)), not because it
cuts; fix that in the shots rather than inventing a link. When a scene change
needs help (a jump in time, a change of mood, two places the viewer must
connect), use the cheapest tool that does the job, in rough order of cost:

- **Sound bridge:** scene B's sound starts under A's last shot, or A's carries
  into B; one music cue spans both. It is made in the edit, so it holds
  whatever the two generations do.
- **Exit and entry**, as above: a subject leaves frame right in A and enters
  frame left in B.
- **Word or question:** A ends on a line that B repeats or answers elsewhere.
- **Light change** on a held frame, for time passing in one place.
- **Dissolve or fade:** for a real jump in time or mood, used sparingly.

**Match cuts by choice only.** A graphic match or object substitution (a shape,
colour or object in A's last frame rhymes with B's first), a motion match, a
foreground wipe or a whip pan into the next scene is a deliberate rhyme, not a
way to join scenes. Use one only where the user asks for it or the story turns
on that rhyme, plan both frames as a pair, and keep it to one or two in a film.
Where one is chosen, it earns its place on a jump in time or place: a shape or
motion that carries over says the two moments belong together.
In generated video the two frames rarely line up, and a near miss reads as a
mistake.

Scenes rarely begin or end static: open with an entrance, a reveal (a door, a
body moving off the lens, a pull-back from a prop) or a voice before its
face, and end with the reverse.

In a narrative film, open a new scene on where and when. A wide, or an insert of a detail that
carries the change (the clock at six, the packed bag by the door), tells the
viewer what changed before the action resumes. *Break it* when the scene
continues straight on from the last, or opens on a detail to reveal the place
later.

## Scene recipes

- **Dialogue:** a wide or opening movement that sets the geography; over-the-
  shoulder reverses at medium; singles closing in toward the peak; reactions
  cut mid-line; a re-establishing shot; a wider shot as they part.
- **Action or fight:** keep each side's direction fixed (hero left to right,
  threat right to left); alternate the hero close with the threat wide; cut on
  impact; build slowly, resolve fast, stop soon after the climax.
- **Chase:** fix pursuer and pursued directions; alternate them; use a head-on
  or tail-away shot to reverse direction legitimately and inserts to compress
  time.
- **Establishing:** outside in (exterior, entrance, character), inside out (a
  detail, then the room), or a move from empty set onto the characters.
- **Reveal:** a move across clues to the payoff; a rack focus, a figure rising
  into frame, a pull-out.
- **Montage:** short shots of selected peaks, one constant element (a
  character, a colour, a direction) and one music cue across them.
- **Point of view:** the looker, what they see, the looker again.

## In generated video

- **Anchor every shot to the references, not to the shot before.** The
  breakdown's wording for each character, prop and set, word for word, and the
  look-dev images on every generation. Each shot is generated from its own
  frame (its storyboard panel or previs, in the prompt's words) and those
  references, as is its keyframe when the user asked for one.
  Leave the previous shot's keyframe and the last frame of its take out of the
  inputs across a CUT: the model keeps that picture's composition, so the
  new angle comes out as the old one moved a little, and the cut reads as a
  jump or an accidental match. The shared references keep the cast, set and
  look consistent across cuts. A retake of the same shot never chains from its
  own rejected take ([iterate on a take](../iterate.md#start-from-the-approved-inputs)).
  A CONTINUE join is not a cut: carry the take's motion into the next segment
  as [continuity](../continuity.md#carry-motion-not-just-a-frame) describes.
- **Write the grammar into the prompt.** Models do not infer the line. State
  the frame side and facing ("Mara frame left, facing right"), the direction of
  travel, the light's direction and time of day, and how the shot begins and
  ends in motion.
- **Write the story as what the camera sees.** Models do not read intent: a
  prompt that says "she realises she has been betrayed" gets a vague face.
  Write the shot's one action from its start state to its end state, with the
  visible change and the face or body that carries the Why ("her jaw
  tightens as she crumples the note in her fist").
- **Chain the states, not the frames.** Open each prompt on its start state,
  which carries on what the shot before ended on in the story (the note still
  in her hand, now seen close), and end it on its end state. Across a CUT the
  state carries in words; only a CONTINUE carries the take itself. With
  keyframes, the start keyframe shows the start state, feeling included; a
  shot that also takes an end keyframe is planned first-last in
  [previs](previs.md#how-previs-feeds-generation). An image-to-video prompt then gives only the motion to the end state, not what
  the still already shows.
- **Generate handles.** Ask for a second or two more than the shot's cut
  length, within the model's duration
  limits.
- **Several shots in one generation.** For tightly coupled coverage of one
  scene (shot and reverse shot, a short action run), models that cut inside a
  clip keep light and identity across the cuts: [Seedance](../models/seedance.md#structure-summary-then-beats),
  [Kling](../models/kling.md#shots), [Veo](../models/veo.md#several-beats-in-one-clip),
  [LTX](../models/ltx.md#multi-shot), [MiniMax H3](../models/minimax-h3.md#minimaxs-structure)
  and [Wan](../models/wan.md#formula).
- **Plan a cover.** Give key scenes an insert or cutaway (a hand, an object, a
  listener) that can hide a seam if a take drifts.
- **Keep things apart in words.** Models merge things that pass close
  together: a camera flies through a rotor, a falling beam passes through a
  wing. Name, positively, where the camera stays for the whole shot ("the
  camera stays outside the rotor disk"), and write a near miss as a gap that
  stays visible ("the boom swings into the space the helicopter has just left,
  a clear gap behind its tail"). Put the contact itself (collision, clipping,
  merged objects) in the model's exclusions as its page describes:
  `negative_prompt` nouns on Veo and Kling 3.0, Wan's negative list, and the
  prompt itself on Kling O3.

## Long takes

A shot with no cuts that travels around its subject (a chase, an escape, a
walk through a party) is one continuous camera path through waypoints, one
per beat. Within one generation it is a single prompt; past the model's length it is segments joined by CONTINUE
([continuity](../continuity.md#every-join-is-cut-or-continue)).

- **Write the path as waypoints.** Each beat's waypoint says where the camera has
  travelled relative to the subject (skimming the water below, alongside the
  cockpit, ahead of the nose, under the landing gear), and what the subject
  and the world do on the way there. Write it in the model's format (timed
  beats for Seedance 2.5 and Kling, one flowing paragraph for LTX). Where the
  model page gives a single-take phrase (Wan, Gemini Omni), use it; elsewhere
  write one unbroken action and name no cut. Veo takes one moment per clip, so
  keep its path to one or two waypoints and chain the rest as CONTINUE
  segments.
- **Use the fewest places.** Every distinct place the path passes through (a
  room, a street, a tower face) is where the model rewrites the world: the fewer
  places a generation passes through, the more often it holds, and a path through
  four held in none of ten takes. Tell the story with the
  fewest places it needs. One generation holds one place; a path that crosses
  into another place (air into water, a street into a room) is a
  [built take](#build-a-long-take-from-segments) whose crossings each happen
  inside a segment, mid-move, never at a join. Never pass more than two keyframe
  stills into one generation: it fades between them instead of moving.
- **Tie the places together in one sentence.** A positive geography anchor that
  holds from the first second ("the glass tower stands at the end of the avenue,
  visible from the moment the camera leaves the window"). Where the path has
  keyframe stills, generating the later ones from the first may help them show
  one place.
- **Don't pin the middle.** A middle keyframe, or a split at a waypoint into
  separate generations, moves the rewrite to the join rather than removing it;
  a first-and-last-frame split also slows into the middle still and pauses there
  unless the outgoing take is cut before the settle
  ([first and last frame](../continuity.md#carry-motion-not-just-a-frame)).
  To hold a path through more places, build the take, or on a model without
  extension split it that way.
- **Open partway through the action.** State what has already happened before
  the first frame ("already hovering just clear of the helipad when the
  platform begins failing"), so the clip doesn't spend its seconds on setup.
- **Each beat causes the next.** The danger that ends one beat drives the
  subject's response in the next (a pipe ruptures, so the aircraft moves out;
  a crane tips across its path, so it sidesteps down). A beat with nothing to
  respond to becomes waiting or slow motion.
- **Give each beat room.** Start from about one beat per three to four
  seconds, then follow the model page's timing guidance: Seedance 2.5 adds
  cuts or drops beats when a range is overfilled, and turns spare seconds into
  waiting or slow motion. Put the peak in the last beat and end on a wider, settled frame that
  shows how it came out.
- **Direct physics and light as well as the look.** Weight and motion belong in
  the style line ("convincing aircraft inertia, realistic rotor motion, immense
  industrial scale"). Name the palette once. Keep
  practical lights at the edge of the path, named as local light ("a small brass
  lamp glows at the frame edge"); a camera swept past one grades the whole frame.
- **Spend words on what the camera sees.** Hype ("epic", "ultra-cinematic")
  adds nothing the beats don't; set resolution in the model's field where it
  has one, not in the prompt.

Review a long take with the [one-take checks](../review.md#one-take-checks), on
two or more takes.

### Build a long take from segments

A path through more places than one generation holds is built from approved
output, one segment at a time: by extending it where the model can (below), or
on a model without extension (MiniMax H3) from first-and-last-frame segments.
There, the first segment starts on the opening still and each later one on the
frame where the kept take before it was cut, still moving, in the next wave; each
ends on an approved still drawn just past its crossing, at the join (underwater
mid-glide, airborne mid-climb), and is generated about a second long so it can
be cut before it settles ([first and last frame](../continuity.md#carry-motion-not-just-a-frame)).
On either route:

- **About 5 s and one place or one crossing per segment, every segment the same length.** Each
  segment's prompt carries enough camera travel for its seconds, and about the
  same travel as its neighbours, so the camera's speed holds across the joins; a
  segment with too little travel fills the rest with a hover.
- **One plain paragraph per segment, 50 to 80 words, no timed beats.** This
  replaces the waypoints and timed beats above: say where the camera goes through
  this one place and what it arrives at, then close on the palette and film look the brief set.
  ("Extend @Video1 as the same single unbroken shot. The camera descends from the
  window over the wet avenue and skims just above the heads of a varied crowd
  crossing at an everyday walking pace, in rust, sage, denim and camel coats. The
  glass office tower at the end of the avenue grows steadily larger ahead. Soft
  green-cyan dusk light, warm amber lamps, 35mm film.")
- **Gate each segment before extending.** No cut or scene swap other than the planned crossing, performed on screen, and its last
  frame shows what the next segment needs (the window, the street ahead),
  including any new subject it arrives at (the crowd, the team). Retake only
  the segment that fails.
- **Move, don't rush.** Describe a change of place as the camera's path, never
  with speed verbs ("dives", "races", "gaining speed"); speed invites a blur
  that hides a swap.
- **Describe new people with variety:** an age range and distinct clothing
  ("late 20s to early 40s, in rust, sage, denim and camel coats"), never just
  "the same people".
- **Extend on Seedance 2.5:** `bytedance/seedance-2.5/reference-to-video` with
  `task: "extension"` ([Seedance](../models/seedance.md#edit-and-extend-wording)),
  at 720p. Extend the whole approved take so far (the segments joined), not only
  its last segment. Image-to-video has no extension, and Veo `extend-video` extends only a Veo-made
  clip.
- **Concatenate the segments.** An extension returns only the new part; join
  the segments in order, re-encoding when their frame sizes differ by a pixel
  or two. Join extensions with straight cuts, never a crossfade: a blend
  overlaps the frames and the camera jumps ahead. Step through each join in the
  exported video for a one-frame hitch.

# Film types

A film is one or more of these types. The type changes what goes into each
stage, never which stages there are or how they lock (at the `own` pace, the
stages are tools the user calls on). Record the types in
`film/TREATMENT.md`'s front matter (`types: [commercial, narrative]`), the lead
type first.

## Narrative

A story with characters across several scenes, 1–3 minutes unless the brief
says otherwise. It takes the stages as written, starting at the treatment,
whose [story rules](treatment.md#what-makes-the-story-work) it follows. It
adds, as the lead type or not:

- **Treatment:** the arc shows as a repeated situation met with a changed
  action (Piper's wave, La Luna's broom).
- **Shot list:** narration, if any, is written before the shots and carries
  only the abstract (a memory, a time jump), never the turn or its cause.
- **Edit and mix:** one music track, shaped to the story's acts.

## Commercial

A commercial starts on [quick ad](../quick-ad.md), a first MiniMax H3 cut with
no stages. These additions apply when the user asks for the staged process, or
when a staged film is also an ad.

- **Treatment:** the one thing the viewer should remember, the audience, the
  call to action and the brand's mandatories (logo, tagline, legal line,
  packshot) the user supplies. Never invent a claim
  or price; a tagline you write goes in the treatment, marked as yours.
- **Breakdown:** the product and logo are supplied references, never generated;
  note what is composited in the edit (logo, end card, legal line, exact label).
- **Shot list:** a packshot and an end card with their exact duration and text;
  the cutdowns and delivery aspect ratios the user asked for, marking which shots
  each cutdown keeps.

## Viral

A viral piece starts on [quick ad](../quick-ad.md) too; these additions apply
when the user asks for the staged process.

- **Treatment:** name the platform. [video styles](../../../video-styles/SKILL.md)
  has established internet formats.
- **Shot list:** on-screen text with its exact
  words and hold time, the loop point if it loops, and text and faces placed for the
  platform's controls ([interface-safe composition](../social-safe-areas.md)).
- **Breakdown and look development:** a recurring character or mascot is
  designed for a series, not one clip.

## Product film

A product film starts on [quick ad](../quick-ad.md) too; these additions apply
when the user asks for the staged process.

- **Treatment:** what the product is, the one quality the film shows (a

  is software belongs to [make-product-demo](../../../make-product-demo/SKILL.md).
- **Breakdown:** the product from the user's photos as an exact reference: its
  shape, colour, materials, label and markings, measured against a hand. Labels
  and logos are composited from the supplied files, never regenerated.
- **Look development:** the product in the style key from the supplied photos,
  checked against them for shape and markings before it is locked.
- **Previs:** hero moves (macro passes, turntables, reveals) in Blender from a
  supplied or sourced model when one exists; [product hero](../../../make-product-demo/references/product-hero.md)
  has the Blender pitfalls.

# Generation routes

Stage 5 of [staged production](staged-production.md#generation): the route each shot
takes and the stage's block.

## Routes

- **Reference-to-video**, the default: the shot from its references and
  prompt ([step 2](staged-production.md#generation)).
- **Image-to-video**: a shot with an approved keyframe animates that still.
  Its prompt is motion only.
- **First-last**: a shot that is one clear action from a start state to an
  end state (a door closes, a character turns to camera, a product lands on
  the table), where a first frame alone leaves the end to chance and a
  Blender clip is too much setup. Animate the start keyframe as the first
  frame and the end keyframe as the last, at the shot's duration within the
  model's range (Seedance 2.5 takes 4–30s). The prompt describes only the
  motion between the two frames, not what is already in them.
  The keyframes are the take's first and last frames, so a first-last shot
  gets no spare handles: anything past the cut plays after the end state.
  Generate the J-cut lead, plus the cut length, plus the outgoing dissolve
  or fade's length and the L-cut trail, each only when the shot's joins
  have one, rounded up to a duration the model takes. Prompt the action to
  leave the start state at the lead and reach the end state at the lead
  plus the cut length, then hold or settle there to the last frame (for a
  4 s cut with a 1 s trail: "the hatch is fully open by 4 s and stays
  open"). When its Into next is CONTINUE, the end state is a moment the move
  passes through: no hold and no trail; generate about a second past the cut
  length, and cut the take while still moving, before that second
  ([carry motion](../continuity.md#carry-motion-not-just-a-frame)). In the edit the clip's `start` is the lead and its `duration` the
  cut length, plus the dissolve's length as
  [assembly](../assembly.md#transitions-and-overlapping-sound) adds it, so
  the end state shows at full strength when the dissolve or the trail
  begins.
- **Previs clip**: use a reference-to-video mode (Seedance 2.5
  `task: "reference"`), the clip as `@Video1` beside the shot's references,
  as [previs](previs.md#how-previs-feeds-generation) describes.
- **Continuation**: a CONTINUE segment extends the kept take before it
  (Seedance 2.5 `task: "extension"`, Veo 3.1 `extend-video`, 720p only) or takes that take's last few seconds as a video reference. It depends on that take, so a CONTINUE run
  generates in waves: the first segments of every run in one batch, the
  next segments once their takes are kept. The cost estimate covers every
  wave; each wave is its own batch under the cost rules.
- **Several shots in one clip**: tightly coupled shots of one scene (a shot
  and its reverse, a short run of action) can be one generation on a model that cuts inside a clip. Write each shot in the model's multi-shot syntax from its page; the clip
  is cut back into its shot IDs in the edit, at the `in` and `out` the
  block records for each shot (below).

multi-shot clip's on its first entry), the `keyframes` card's approval carries the

from the image estimate, so the card prices each redo) appear only on a shot the
user asked keyframes for. A continuation has `"mode": "extension"` or
`"mode": "reference"` with the previous take in `inputs`. A first-last shot
(SC01-S02) has `"mode": "first-last"`, its start keyframe in `keyframe` and its
end in `keyframeEnd`, both also in `inputs`.

A multi-shot clip keeps one entry per shot it covers, each with
`"mode": "multi-shot"`, `clip` set to the clip's first shot ID, and the
clip's model, prompt, inputs and whole `durationSeconds`; `cost` goes on the
first entry only. When a take is kept, every entry gets the same `keptTake`,
plus its `in` and `out`: the seconds in the clip where that shot starts and
ends. Measure them from the take's actual cuts (FFmpeg `scdet`), which drift from
the prompt's timing. In the edit, each shot's clip `start` and `duration` stay inside
its `in` and `out`.

## Keyframe pairs

The two keyframes of a first-last shot are one moment of one action, as
[previs](previs.md#how-previs-feeds-generation) plans them. A CONTINUE segment's pair may span the one crossing its
move performs on screen (air into water): split after the crossing, never at it.

Across a CUT, the next shot's start keyframe comes from its own frame and
references ([step 2](staged-production.md#generation)).

# Look development

Stage 4a, alongside [storyboard frames or optional technical previs](previs.md).
Settle how the film looks before any shot is generated: one style key for the
film, a scoped look for any scenes or shots the treatment gives their own look,
and a reference image for
every character, set and key prop in the breakdown.

## Style key

The style key is the look in words plus one image that shows it: one
representative frame from the film in that style, generated with
[make-image](../../../make-image/SKILL.md)'s default at the film's aspect ratio.

Offer two or three distinct style keys when the user has not fixed the look,
each as words and an image, with a cost estimate before generating them.

## Scoped looks

A film can mix looks on purpose: a photoreal flashback in an animated film, a
look per chapter. Each `scopedLook` in treatment piece 1.6 becomes a look here,
its words plus one image made as the style key's is, applying to the scenes
(`SC02`) or shots (`SC02-S01`) it names; no scene or shot takes two. A
character, set or prop seen under a scoped look also gets a reference in that
look, its file name ending in the look's ID (`CH01-flashback.png`).

## Moodboard

The user can give a moodboard: images, frames from films, paintings,
photographs that show the look they want. When the look is open, say they can;
they drop the images into the chat or point to files or a folder. Copy each
into `supplied/mood/` in the project, beside the other supplied files, and
describe in a line what it gives (`supplied/mood/harbour.jpg`: cold blue dusk,
sodium light, heavy grain).

A mood reference supplies the look only: palette, light, lens, grain and
texture. Never its subject, a face, a composition or anything of its story.
The two kinds of reference never swap roles:

- A mood reference never carries identity into a shot. Describe its look in
  the style key's words; the people, places and objects in it stay out of
  every prompt and every reference image.
- An identity reference (a supplied photo of a person, product or place) never
  sets the look ([hold the style key](#hold-the-style-key)).

Draw the two or three style key candidates from the moodboard, each naming the mood references it draws from. A
candidate image may take a mood reference as a style input, with the prompt
saying it gives the look only: "Use image 2 only for its palette, light and
grain; nothing in it appears in the frame." The moodboard is recorded in
treatment piece 1.6 ([the pieces](treatment.md#the-story-piece-by-piece)) and in
`film/LOOKDEV.md` (`moodRefs`, and each candidate's `moodFrom`).

## Reference images

Recurring characters use [Project Cast](../cast.md): reuse an approved card or
draft a hero portrait, a separate full body and a fixed description before
shots. Save them with `cast.create` (or revise with Cast commands), show the
card and ask the user to approve it (in chat or the Cast panel). Map each breakdown ID
to its Cast ID in `film/LOOKDEV.md`. A supplied identifiable person's photos
need `origin: "real-person"` and their actual consent record.

For each character, outfit, set and key prop in the breakdown, generate a
reference in the style key: a character as a full-body front view plus a face
close-up on a plain background, a set as an empty wide view in its main light, a
prop alone on a plain background. Use the breakdown's wording for the subject
and the style key's words for the look. A user-supplied photo of a person,
product or place is an identity reference only: redraw it in the style key and
keep the photo for identity (see [hold the style key](#hold-the-style-key)).
Generation makes each shot from these references and the Cast cards, with no
keyframe unless the user asks for one.

Estimate the batch before generating
([paid generation](../craft/paid-generation.md)). Save them under `film/lookdev/` with the element's ID in the file name
(`CH01-W1.png`, `SE01.png`). While they generate, build technical previs only
for shots whose motion needs it; otherwise draw hand-drawn storyboard frames
([board style](../storyboard.md#board-style)). Explain any grey blocking before building it and show it together with
the style frames ([previs](previs.md)). Ask what it needs from the user
(a mockup clip's cost) as [paid generation](../craft/paid-generation.md#submit-and-wait) describes; the
references are approved with the previs, once they are shown. At the `run`
pace, decide it yourself and say so in one line; a paid mockup clip above the
user's spend limit still waits for their approval.

That approval locks the film stage only. Character cards always wait for the
user's approval (in chat or the Cast panel), including at `run` / `own` pace;
approve a card only on their word (unless `<voyager_autopilot>` tells you to make every decision
yourself: see [Project Cast](../cast.md)). Changing refs, description, style or provenance makes
an approved card draft again; a scoped-look or outfit revision to a card also
needs the user's approval again. Every later image/video request uses its approved
`cast` IDs; the adapter selects identity refs for the model.

## `film/LOOKDEV.md`

The style key (its words and image path), each scoped look with its scenes or
shots, the moodboard, if any, with what
each mood reference gives and which candidate drew on it, then a table of every
breakdown ID with its reference path, the prompt and job ID, and which supplied
photo, if any, it takes identity from. Put the style key image and every
reference image in the approval question as Markdown images with their absolute
paths, as still approval does.

Keep character-to-Cast ID mappings and current card status in the prose;
`cast.show` is the authority for approval. Report likeness verdicts
or an unavailable check rather than claiming that a stage lock verifies faces.

A redo or a changed prompt on one reference regenerates only that image, in
the style key; the prompt the user typed is used word for word. Record each
reference's `cost`, what regenerating it costs, so it is shown with the image.

## Hold the style key

Once look development is locked, the look that applies to a shot wins over every
other input, as
[the style key wins](../prompting.md#the-style-key-wins-over-photo-references) says:
the scoped look naming the shot or its scene (the shot's own first), and the style
key everywhere else. A frame in its scoped look is on look, not a drifted take.
The style key stands for the moodboard: mood references are not passed to
reference images or shots.

# Film: my way

At `own`, do what the user asks, in the order they ask, from what they give
you. Nothing on the list of stages is mandatory and no stage waits on another:

- **No story process.** No story pieces, no structure pitch, no
  `film/TREATMENT.md` unless they ask for one. Their script, shot list or notes
  stay in their words; raise a problem as a note beside them, never by
  rewriting them.
- **Stages are tools.** Write a stage file only when the user asks for it
  ("give me a shot list", "break down the characters") or when consistency
  needs it: a character, prop or set that appears in more than one shot gets
  a breakdown entry so its wording is reused word for word in every prompt.
  The file has the same shape as at the other paces, built from what exists
  and the user's words rather than from locked stages above it, so `voyager
film card` shows it on its own. Show it in full and lock it by updating the stage file's front matter, with no
  approval question. A change the user asks for reopens it, as at the other paces.
- **Offered, not required.** Offer a style key and reference images for
  recurring elements in one line when they would help; go on without them when the
  user declines or ignores the offer. Previs only when asked. Recurring
  characters use [Project Cast](../cast.md): reuse or draft a card, then ask the
  user to approve it (in chat or the Cast panel) before shots. `own` skips stage
  reviews, not Cast approval; approve a card only on their word (`<voyager_autopilot>` aside: see
  [Project Cast](../cast.md)).
- **What still holds.** The spend gate, where an estimate above the spend limit in
  `<voyager_creative_preferences>` stops for their answer ([paid
  generation](../craft/paid-generation.md)); shots generated from their
  references, with keyframes only when asked and those anchored on the
  references rather than chained from the shot before across a cut; CUT or
  CONTINUE motion across joins
  ([generation](staged-production.md#generation)); approved `cast` IDs on every
  image/video estimate and run containing the character; and the user's words verbatim,
  with `userEdited` on any stage file.

# Previs

Stage 4b, alongside [look development](look-dev.md). Only build technical previs
when motion precision matters: complex camera moves, multi-character blocking,
precise spatial relationships or continuous action. For simple or static shots,
and style-led pieces (anime, illustrated), default to hand-drawn storyboard
frames ([board style](../storyboard.md#board-style)). Offer grey previs only for shots whose motion needs it; at `own`,
previs only when asked ([my way](my-way.md)).

Before building any grey previs, tell the user in one line: "Grey blocking to
lock camera and movement; it won't look like the final film. The look-dev frames
carry the style." Keep technical blocking grayscale.

## Choose a route per shot

- **Storyboard frame**: the default for a simple or static shot, hand-drawn as
  [board style](../storyboard.md#board-style) says: the characters' Cast
  references for identity only, the set in words. Record it as the `frame`
  route in `film/PREVIS.md`; no grey blockout or clip is needed. A change to the
  film's look leaves hand-drawn frames as they are. Frames drawn in a style the
  user asked for are redrawn when that style changes, only the affected ones.
- **Blender**, through [edit-in-blender](../../../edit-in-blender/SKILL.md): for a
  complex camera move, multi-character blocking, a precise spatial relationship
  or a continuous action. Render grayscale (Workbench, solid shading, no
  textures).
- **Grayscale mockup clip**: when proxies cannot carry the action (a gesture, a
  face turning, water). A short grayscale clip, from Blender or a cheap draft
  generation such as Seedance's 480p draft, estimated and approved like any
  paid take, that shows only the motion.
- **Blocking frame**: only when a technical composition reference is needed,
  one grayscale frame at the shot's framing, also the `frame` route.

When technical previs is needed, previs a run of shots joined by CONTINUE
([continuity](../continuity.md)) as one clip across the whole run, with its
segment boundaries marked; generation cuts it into a motion reference per segment.

Every shot ends with at least one still for the storyboard: a storyboard or
blocking frame is its own still, and a clip's grayscale start frame (`startFrame`)
is the still for a Blender or mockup shot.

## How previs feeds generation

A previs clip becomes the motion input; the shot's set and prop images (and its
keyframe, when the user asked for keyframes) are additional appearance inputs. Recurring characters come
from approved [Cast](../cast.md) IDs on the request. Image-to-video cannot take a
clip's motion, so a shot with a previs clip uses reference-to-video; choose
the route with `cast.models`. Seedance 2.5 (`task: "reference"`) is one route on eligible
plans. Describe the roles: "Mara follows the camera movement and blocking of
the previs clip; do not copy its grey shapes or lighting. Draw everything in
the style key's look." The adapter supplies character refs and their token
mapping; do not guess their `@ImageN` positions or hand-list the card's refs. Read
[Seedance](../models/seedance.md) and
[motion-to-video](../../../edit-in-blender/references/motion-to-video.md) before the
first take.
A storyboard or blocking frame instead guides the shot's prompt: its framing,
staging and move go into the words of a
[reference-to-video](../../SKILL.md#generate-shots-from-references) generation,
and the panel stays out of the inputs. When the user asked for keyframes, it is
the composition guide for the shot's keyframe still.

When the user asks for start and end frames, a `frame` shot that is one clear
action from a start state to an end state is planned as first-last: give it both a `startFrame` and an
`endFrame` still in that frame's look, the start and end of the shot-list Action,
and say "first-last" in its notes. The two stills guide the shot's start and end
keyframes, which generation animates as its first and last frame
([first-last](generation.md#routes)). On a Blender or mockup shot,
`startFrame` and `endFrame` stay camera references: the clip carries the
motion.

The two frames are one moment of one action: the same set, light, wardrobe and
lens. Only the subject's pose or position and the camera's position change, and
only as far as the shot's duration and move allow. A pair that changes more (a
new location, a jump in time, several actions) animates into messy in-between
motion: split it into two shots, which reopens the shot list.

## The storyboard

Present previs together with the look-dev frames, never alone; show the style
frames first, then label any grey still or clip as technical blocking.

Show the previs as a storyboard the user flips through, shot by shot, not as a
video of held frames. Put every shot's still in the approval question, in shot
order, as Markdown images with their absolute paths, as still approval does:
Voyager shows them as a grid that opens into a carousel. Before each still, one line names the shot and
its timing and camera:

```md
Approve the look and previs?

**Style key**

![Style key](</absolute/project/films/northfold/lookdev/style-key.png>)

**SC01-S01 — technical blocking** (4 s, 35mm, eye level): push in 1 m; Mara crosses frame left to right.

![SC01-S01](</absolute/project/films/northfold/previs/SC01-S01-start.png>)
```

A first-last shot shows both its stills under its line, start then end.

Present each Blender or mockup clip as well.

A change to one shot's previs redoes only that shot's stills or clip; a
mockup clip is a paid take, estimated first. Recut the animatic, when there is
one, only after a shot in it changed.

## The animatic, on request

Cut an animatic only when the user asks for one, for a previs by name, or for a
check of the film's timing as a whole. It cuts every shot's previs at its shot-list duration, in order,
a blocking frame held for its shot, with the dialogue read as a scratch track or
as on-screen text and the music's tempo marked, into
`film/previs/animatic.mp4`, and present it. Cut it with `voyager media assemble`
([assembly](../assembly.md)), not raw FFmpeg: the app plays only its H.264.

## `film/PREVIS.md`

Per shot: the route, the previs file, the still, the camera (lens, height, move,
start and end frame) and notes for generation. Ask to approve the previs with
the storyboard in the question and the file's path in your reply. Use the
[stage's three options](staged-production.md#approving-a-stage), "Change something (Type below)" among them.

# Shot list

Stage 3. Every shot of the film, built from the locked treatment and breakdown.
A recurring element (one that has to look the same each time it appears) uses
its breakdown ID; a new recurring element goes back into the breakdown, which
reopens it. A one-off background or insert element is described in the shot's
Action and needs no ID.

Plan the shots as a sequence, not as separate clips: how each one joins the
next is part of the shot. Every shot is one step of its scene's change in the
treatment, caused by the shot before it or answering it, and leading into the
next; most cuts make a pair ([cut in pairs](cinematography.md#cut-in-pairs)).
[Cinematography grammar](cinematography.md) has the defaults; the breakdown's camera language overrides them where the user's
style differs. [Continuity](../continuity.md) decides which joins are cuts at
all: a shot ID is a waypoint segment, and two IDs joined by CONTINUE play as
one unbroken take.

## `film/SHOTLIST.md`

A table per scene, one row per shot, IDs that never change (`SC01-S01`):

| Shot | Title | Framing | Angle | Move | Duration | Action | Elements | Dialogue / text | Sound | Into next | Why |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| SC01-S01 | The note | wide | eye level | slow push | 4 s | Mara steps into the dark kitchen and picks up the note | CH01-W1, PR02, SE01 | none | fridge hum; paper rustle | CUT | she is alone with the note, so the knock in S02 frightens her |

- **Title:** two to four plain words naming the shot. Approvals and the
  presented takes show it beside the shot.
- **Duration:** the shot's length in the cut, in whole seconds; the scene's
  shots add up to its breakdown duration. A shot longer than the planned model
  can generate, or one that crosses into another place more than once, is split into
  segments, one row and ID each, joined by CONTINUE, each join inside a place and
  never at a crossing;
  each row's Duration is its segment's length in the cut. Never cut it short or
  give it a cut it does not need. Generation adds handles on top where the model's range allows.
- **Action:** one simple action the camera can see, by at most two characters
  (anyone else is background), with no fine hand work and no readable text in
  the generated picture (titles and cards go on in the edit). A plot point is a physical change on screen (the
  note tears, the door locks), never a thought or a feeling to infer; a shot
  with two actions is two shots. It starts and ends in motion where it can; a shot that holds still at its end is a
  choice the Why explains, not the default.
- **Elements:** the breakdown IDs of the recurring elements in frame. A one-off
  is described in the Action instead.
- **Sound:** the shot's foley and any line, and whether music plays.
- **Into next:** `CUT` or `CONTINUE:` first ([continuity](../continuity.md#every-join-is-cut-or-continue)).
  A plain `CUT` is the default and needs nothing after it. Add how, in a few
  plain words, only when the cut carries something the edit must do: L-cut (her
  line runs over the next shot), J-cut, sound bridge, half-second dissolve; or,
  for CONTINUE, the move and action that carry on. Give a dissolve or fade its
  length. Name a match cut or match on action only where the user asked for one
  or the story turns on it ([joining scenes](cinematography.md#joining-scenes)).
  The last shot of a scene is a plain `CUT` into the next scene unless the scene
  change needs a link, a `ruleBreak` or the camera language says otherwise.
  A subject who carries on into the next scene's place on screen (through the
  door, into the water) is one `CONTINUE:` run: the crossing plays inside one
  segment, and the join comes after it, inside the new place.
- **Why:** the shot's story purpose and its links: what the viewer learns or
  feels here that the scene's change needs, and what leads into it and out of
  it ("the glass shatters: the result of her throw in S02"). Never only a camera reason.

The block adds, per shot, what generation needs to keep the story and the
joins: the `beat` (the label of the treatment beat the shot advances), the
`frame` (who is on which side, facing and moving which way), the `startState`
and `endState` (pose, position and light at the first and last frame, what is
now true in the story, and how the protagonist feels: "the note in her hand,
the door open, afraid"), the
`soundOverlap` (what sound leads into or carries over the cut, whether it is
a take's own sound or a bed, and by how long) and, for a deliberate break of a default, the `ruleBreak`. These stay in
the block and the prose below the tables; the table shows Into next.

After the table: the cue map (the music's tempo, sections and the beats that cuts
and key actions land on) and any scene transition other than a plain cut.

## Changes

A change to one shot changes only that shot, and a redo redrafts only it,
keeping its `userEdited` fields. A shot's dialogue is the treatment's: changing
it reopens the treatment's scenes piece. An added or split shot takes the next
free number in its scene; no other shot is renumbered. Check the runtime again
after any change.

## Check before asking for approval

- Runtime matches the treatment's target; every spoken line in the treatment is in exactly one shot.
- In a narrative film, every shot advances its beat: its Why names the cause
  it answers and the effect it sets up. Cut a shot with no story purpose; move
  or rewrite one with no link.
- Every Action keeps to the Action rule above, unless a `ruleBreak` says
  otherwise.
- A setup the story pays off later (a motif, a planted object) is framed so
  the viewer sees it, in a shot whose Why names the payoff.
- In a narrative film, every shot has a `beat`, a `startState` and an `endState`, and each
  `startState` carries on the story state the shot before ended in, seen from
  its own angle across a CUT; what a scene changed stays changed in the next.
- Every shot but the last has an Into next that starts `CUT` or `CONTINUE:`.
  A plain cut between scenes is fine and needs no link; a scene boundary gets
  one only when the change needs help, such as a jump in time or mood
  ([joining scenes](cinematography.md#joining-scenes)).
- Match cuts and match on action appear only where the user asked for them or
  the story turns on them.
- Every CUT has a reason in the story or the rhythm; a cut that exists only
  because a clip ends is a CONTINUE. Within a scene most cuts make a pair
  (action and result, a look and what is seen) and the sizes step in toward
  its peak. In a narrative film, a new scene opens on a shot that says where
  and when (a wide, or an insert of a telling detail), unless it continues
  into the scene or the camera language says otherwise.
- Screen direction, eyelines and light carry across each cut within a scene,
  unless a `ruleBreak` or the camera language says otherwise.
- Across a CUT, adjacent shots of the same subject change angle or size
  clearly, unless a `ruleBreak` or the camera language says otherwise (a
  deliberate jump cut). Across a CONTINUE, framing changes only as the move carries it; the
  move's speed and direction and the action carry on unchanged.
- A `soundOverlap` that carries a sound over the cut comes from something
  this shot shows by its `endState` (the hatch clangs open, and the ring
  carries over the next shot). A sound whose cause comes after the end state
  belongs to the next shot; move it there or change the end state.

          "endState": "the note in her hand, turning toward the window light, uneasy, the push still moving",
          "intoNext": "CUT",

        }

    }
  ],
  "cueMap": {

    "sections": [{ "name": "Intro", "shots": ["SC01-S01"], "note": "piano alone" }],

  },

`dialogue` is the line or on-screen text exactly, or `""`. A shot's `music`,
`frame`, `intoNext`, `soundOverlap` and `ruleBreak`, the cue map's fields and
`typeInputs` are optional; so are `beat`, `startState` and `endState`, except
in a narrative film. `transitions` holds the
links between scenes that need more than a plain cut, or `[]`; a join inside a
scene is its shot's `intoNext`. `typeInputs` holds what the
film's types add to the shot list ([film types](film-types.md)): the packshot
and end card, cutdowns, text holds and the loop point, if it loops.

# Produced film: staged production

At the `review` and `run` paces, draft each stage, show it
in full, get it locked, then start the next one without being asked. Who locks
it follows the film's [check-in pace](#check-in-pace). At the `review` and
`run` paces the stages apply to every film, whatever the length or the user's
experience; an expert changes what goes into a stage, never whether it happens.
A user with their own plan works at the `own` pace instead.

A brief that is one shot (a single clip, one image to animate, a loop of one
action) is not a film: follow [make-ai-video](../../SKILL.md#match-the-process-to-the-piece)'s single clip path for it
and say so in one line, even when a film kind was chosen. A user who wants a
film of several shots without the stages ("I have my own plan, just help me
generate") is at the `own` pace.

## Check-in pace

Before stage 1, settle how the user wants to work and record it in
`film/pace.json`: `{ "pace": "review" }`, `{ "pace": "run" }` or
`{ "pace": "own" }`.

- **review:** the user approves each stage, as below. The default.
- **run:** each stage is still shown in full, but you lock it and go on.
- **own:** the user's instructions are the plan. No stage happens unless they
  ask for it or it is needed to keep the film consistent. Read [my
  way](my-way.md) before acting at `own`, and again when resuming at it.

Infer it from the brief. "Just make it", "skip the approvals" or "decide
everything for me" is `run`, as is a `<voyager_autopilot>` block telling you to make every decision yourself; a brief that asks to see each stage is `review`;
"I know what I want", "I have my own shot list (or script)", "skip the process"
or "just help me generate" is `own`. A brief with both ("I have my own plan,
just make it") is `own`, and its "just make it" also skips still review.
Otherwise it stays `review` until the story's review question, whose "Just
make it" option sets `run` ([how the user reviews the
story](treatment.md#how-the-user-reviews-the-story)); never ask a separate
question for it. When `film/pace.json` exists, never ask
again; a film without one is at `review`. The user can change the pace at any
point ("just finish it", "let me see each stage from here"): rewrite the file
and go on at the new pace from the current stage.

At `run`, do steps 1 and 2 of [approving a stage](#approving-a-stage) without
the question, then lock it by updating its front matter as in step 5 and start
the next stage in the same turn; images a stage would put in its question go in
the reply. Lock the treatment only after its [story
check](treatment.md#check-the-story-before-showing-it).
Where a stage would offer the user alternatives, pick one yourself and say
which in one line. Go on this way to the finished edit. The spend gate still asks:
an estimate above the spend limit in `<voyager_creative_preferences>` stops for their answer ([paid
generation](../craft/paid-generation.md)), and every estimate is stated in a
line of your reply. A change the user sends reopens its stage as in [changing
a locked stage](#approving-a-stage).

## Approving a stage

Every stage file starts with this front matter:

```yaml
---
stage: breakdown
status: draft # draft | locked | stale
version: 2
locked: 2026-10-05 # only when locked
basedOn: { treatment: 3 } # the locked versions it was built from
userEdited: { CH01: [features] } # fields the user wrote, by item ID
---
```

Text the user typed for an item's field goes into the stage word for word, and
the field's name goes under the item's ID in `userEdited`; no redraft ever
rewrites a `userEdited` field.

1. Draft the stage and write it to its file as `draft`.
2. Put the whole stage in your reply as Markdown, never just a link to the file. A long stage gets a short summary first, then
   the full content. The question text is one short line in plain words that
   names the stage and starts with "Approve" ("Approve the story?", "Approve the
   shot list?"), never the stage itself: a question without "Approve" can be answered automatically. "Lock" is this file's word for
   approved, not the user's: never put it in the question or an option.
   Write that reply as visible text before you call the question tool: the
   user sees your reply text and the card, never your thinking or the file.
3. Ask with the host's question tool, one question, these three options, each
   with a description that says what happens next, and **no option marked
   "(Recommended)"**:
   - "Approve, start the <next stage>" (for example "Approve, start the
     breakdown"): "Marks this stage approved and starts the <next stage> now."
   - "Change something (Type below)": "Type what to change. Only that changes,
     then you see this stage again."
   - "Try another direction (Type below, optional)": "A different take on this
     stage: the direction you type, or left blank, 2–3 short ones to pick from.
     This draft is kept."
4. **End the turn.** At the `review` pace, only an explicit approval locks a stage. After the question
   tool call, write nothing until the user's answer arrives: never restate the
   stage, even when the tool returns before the user answers. When the answer
   comes back in the same turn, act on it as below. An answer to another
   question or a "looks good" about part of it is not an approval. When the
   user says to just go, skip approvals or decide for them from here on, that
   sets the pace to `run`: rewrite `film/pace.json`, make any choices left,
   lock this stage and go on at that [pace](#check-in-pace). A "you pick" on
   one choice makes that choice and keeps the pace.
5. **Approve:** edit the stage's front matter to `status: locked`, `locked` to
   today's date and `basedOn` to the locked dependency versions. Keep the treatment's
   piece versions. Then **start the next stage in the same turn** and end at its question.
6. **Change something:** change only what the user wrote in the text box and
   nothing else in the stage, write the file (still `draft`), then show the
   revised stage in full and ask the same question with the same three options.
   With an empty text box, change nothing: ask in one plain line what they want
   changed and end the turn.
7. **Try another direction:** first keep the current draft as a version: copy
   its file to `film/versions/` under a name no earlier copy has
   (`TREATMENT-draft-1.md`, then `-draft-2`). When the text box names a
   direction, draft that one. When it is empty, offer 2–3 alternatives of a few
   lines each with the question tool ("Which direction do you approve?", no
   option marked "(Recommended)"), end the
   turn, and draft the one the user picks. Write the new draft to the stage file,
   show it in full and ask the stage's question again.

The next stage the approve option names: treatment → breakdown → shot list →
look development and previs → generation → the edit. Look development and previs
are drafted together and shown for approval together, in one question ("Approve
the look and previs?") whose approve option is "Approve, start generation".
Resuming reads only the stage files in `film/`, never `film/versions/`.

The user may approve several drafted stages in one answer, or bring a stage they
wrote themselves (their script, their shot list): write it to its file, fill
what the stage needs and ask them to approve it like any other.

**Stage 1 is built in pieces.** At `own`, only when the user asks for the
story process. The story is drafted in six pieces, each saved
as `film/pieces/<id>.json`: 1.1 logline and benchmark, 1.2 characters, 1.3
world and tone, 1.4 beats, 1.5 scenes and script, 1.6 look and style refs.
At the `review` pace, before 1.1, ask once how the user wants to review the
story ("Draft it all, I'll review at the end", suggested as the fastest,
"Walk me through it" or "Just make it", which sets the pace to `run`), and record the answer in
`film/story-review.json` so it is never asked again in this project. At `run`, draft them all at once without asking. Walked
through, each piece is approved on its own with the steps above, one question
per piece, before the next is drafted from it. Drafted all at once, the six are
written in one go, each `approved` with `autoApproved: true`, and the user
reviews the assembled treatment. Keep them in your task list (TaskCreate or
TodoWrite in Claude, `update_plan` in Codex). When all six are approved, assemble the treatment with
the approved pieces, preserving approved text word for word, then approve the treatment as a stage.
Reopening a piece makes every piece built on it stale. [Treatment and
script](treatment.md#the-story-piece-by-piece) has the pieces, their
files and their questions.

**Changing a locked stage.** The user can reopen any stage. Reopening sets the stage to `draft`, keeping its `version` while no stage
built on it is written; otherwise it bumps the `version` and marks every
written stage built on it `stale`: say which ones. After the reopened stage locks again, update each stale stage from its new
inputs, keeping what still holds, and lock it again before going further down.
Never silently edit a locked file.

**Resuming.** At the start of each turn in a film project, read
`film/pace.json` first. At `own`, read what exists in `film/`, sum it up in one
line, and follow the user's last instruction rather than the stage order.
Otherwise read the front matter of every stage file in `film/` and
continue from the first stage that is not
locked; before the treatment is locked, read `film/pieces/` and continue from
the first piece that is not approved; with all six stage files locked, the film is in the edit. Tell the user where the film stands in one line when you resume.

## The stage block

Each stage file holds the stage twice: right after the front matter, a fenced
`film-stage` block with the stage as JSON, then the stage as prose. Voyager
shows the stage from the block, and shows the prose instead when the block is
missing or does not parse; you and the user read the prose. Each stage's
reference gives its block's shape; [film types](film-types.md) gives
the `typeInputs` each type adds. The front matter's `stage` is the block's
`stage`: `treatment`, `breakdown`, `shot-list`, `look-dev`, `previs` or
`generation`.

- Durations are numbers of seconds; every other value is text, a list or true/false.
- Every field the shape shows, in the same words as the prose: the same IDs,
  the same lines of dialogue. Leave out an optional field rather than write
  "none"; a scene with no lines has `"script": []`.
- Every change to the stage changes both, in the same edit. The treatment's
  block and prose preserve the approved pieces; change its pieces
  instead.
- Change the block by editing the file in place with your file edit tool,
  never with a regex or string-substitution script, which can turn the JSON's
  `\n` escapes into raw line breaks. After the edit, read the block back and
  confirm it parses as JSON before running `voyager film card`.

Settle the film's type: narrative, commercial, viral or product film, or a mix.

## Generation

Recurring characters need user-approved [Cast](../cast.md) cards. When look
development and previs are both locked (at `own`, as soon as the user asks to
generate: work from what exists, and a missing look or previs is not a gate):

1. Write `film/GENERATION.md` (status `draft`): per take, the model, mode and
   inputs (set and prop refs, previs clip; a keyframe only when asked for), the
   prompt in that model's syntax, duration and the cost. Group the shots into
   takes first, by the shot list's Into next or, at `own`, the user's board:
   panels and shots are waypoints, not clips. An action that runs on across
   them in one place is one CONTINUE take, one generation within the model's
   duration (15 s, or 30 s on Seedance 2.5) from its references or at most two
   stills, and every CUT needs a reason
   ([multi-shot practice](../continuity.md#multi-shot-practice)). A
   frame-accurate board keeps every approved frame as a keyframe instead, a
   segment per pair of consecutive frames ([turn the board into video](../storyboard.md#turn-the-board-into-video)).
   Route with `cast.models`; keep `cast` on every estimate, run and retake.
   Read [generation routes](generation.md) and the model's page in
   [model-aware prompting](../model-prompting.md) first. Each prompt carries the
   shot's joins from the shot list: who is where in frame, facing and moving
   which way, the light's direction and time of day, and the motion it starts and ends in.
   It carries the shot's story too: one camera move and one subject action
   from its `startState` to the `endState` it must land on, the feeling at
   each, and its Why as what the camera sees. Add a second or two of handles
   where the model's range allows. [Cinematography grammar](cinematography.md#in-generated-video)
   has the reasons; a style the camera language set wins over it.
   A CONTINUE run longer than the model's duration, or one that crosses into
   another place, is segments: each segment after the first is the next segment
   of that take, not a new shot: its prompt opens on the state the previous segment ends in, already
   in motion (the camera mid-move, the action mid-phase), with no establishing
   description, and its route carries the motion, not just a frame: the first
   of [continuity's routes](../continuity.md#carry-motion-not-just-a-frame) the
   model allows, the last frame alone only as the fallback. Each crossing falls inside a segment, never
   at a join, and no generation takes more than two keyframe stills. A segment
   that is not an extension or first and last frame generates about a second of
   overlap with the one before.
2. By default a shot has no keyframe: it is generated straight from its references
   ([generate shots from references](../../SKILL.md#generate-shots-from-references)):
   `cast` for its characters, the look-dev images of its sets and props, and a
   prompt with its framing, move, panel staging and look; a set image gives
   the place's design, not the shot's camera. When the user asks for keyframes (stills, start and end frames), generate
   one keyframe still per shot from the locked look and previs frame
   (at `own`, from whatever look and frames exist and the user's words) and
   consider [still review](../stills.md). A frame-accurate board's approved
   frames are already its keyframes: reuse them, and generate a still only for
   a frame it lacks. A first-last shot (a
   `frame` shot that previs planned as first-last) gets two, a start and an end keyframe, from its previs
   `startFrame` and `endFrame`; for review, show them side by side as a pair
   ([keyframe pairs](generation.md#keyframe-pairs)). On a Blender or
   mockup shot those two stills are camera references and do not make it
   first-last. A keyframe prompt carries the words and image of the look that
   applies to its shot: its scoped look, if one names the shot or its scene,
   otherwise the style key. Check every still against that look before showing
   it ([look development](look-dev.md#hold-the-style-key)).
   A CONTINUE segment that extends or references the take before it needs no
   keyframe. On a first-and-last-frame or last-frame route, its first frame is
   that take's last frame, taken in its generation wave once that take is kept;
   it is not a still to approve. A last frame there is the next waypoint's
   approved keyframe; on first-and-last-frame the first frame is where the kept
   take is cut while still moving, before it settles onto that keyframe.
   Generate each keyframe from its own shot: its previs frame, its cast, the
   breakdown references of its elements and the look-dev style references. It
   shows the shot's `startState` (an end keyframe its `endState`).
   Across a CUT, leave out the previous shot's keyframe and a take's last frame,
   or the new angle comes out as the old one moved a little
   ([anchor every shot](cinematography.md#in-generated-video)). A revised
   keyframe changes only its own shot.
3. Generate the takes with `cast`, following make-ai-video for estimates, the
   credit check, submitting the batch and waiting. Each take follows one of the
   [generation routes](generation.md#routes):
   reference-to-video (the default), image-to-video, first-last, a previs clip,
   a continuation, or several shots in one clip.

   While the clips render, ask the edit's open choices (captions, the export
   format) as [paid generation](../craft/paid-generation.md#submit-and-wait)
   describes; an answer there never keeps a take or locks generation. At the
   `run` pace, make those choices yourself and name them in one line.

4. Present each clip with `--deliverable` set to its shot written out
   (`"<film title> · Scene 1 · Shot 1"` for SC01-S01) and `--title` set to
   the shot's title, so retakes stack as versions of that shot, not of the film.
   Record each kept take (job ID, path) per shot in `film/GENERATION.md`. A
   retake changes only that shot. A take or multi-shot clip that covers several
   shots is presented under its first shot ID and recorded against every shot
   it covers; retaking any of them regenerates the whole clip.
   Before keeping a take, watch its joins with the take before it and flag

Stage 1. The story is written with the user, not for them. The shot list gets
its own stage. At the `own` [pace](my-way.md) none of this stage runs

## Write it together

When the brief leaves the story's shape open, open with a short take on the idea and two or
three candidate structures, each in a sentence, with the one you would choose and why. When the
user states a shape (an in-medias-res opening, a loop, a vignette, a mood piece), draft that
shape; don't pitch others.
At the `run` [pace](staged-production.md#check-in-pace), ask nothing: pick the
structure yourself and say which in one line. Draft as soon as the shape is
clear. When the user brings a script, keep their words and structure, and
raise problems as notes beside it rather than rewriting it.

## What makes the story work

Draft every piece to these rules; [the story check](#check-the-story-before-showing-it)
tests them. Another film type, or a shape the user stated (a loop, a vignette,
a mood piece), keeps only the clip rules.

- **Scope.** One protagonist, one dramatic question, no subplots; at most two
  characters on screen at once, one to four places. Decide the ending first,
  start late: the inciting incident lands in the first 15% of the runtime.
- **Logline (1.1).** One sentence: the protagonist, a concrete goal, what stands
  in the way and what is at stake, every noun something a camera can film, and
  an ending it implies. Know the premise as cause and effect ("persistence
  turns imitation into self-expression"). Every alternative passes too.
- **Want and need (1.2).** `want` is a concrete goal visible on screen; `flaw`
  is what in them blocks it; `arc` reads want → need → change ("wants to copy
  the masters → needs her own eye → paints the sea as she sees it"). The climax
  forces a choice between want and need, and the protagonist's own action
  settles it. Coincidence may cause trouble, never end it.
- **Scene budget (1.4, 1.5).** About 15–30 s a scene: 60 s is two to four
  scenes, two to three minutes four to six scenes and five to nine beats. Under
  45 s a story is the want, one attempt and the choice. When the story needs
  more, make it smaller.
- **Beats (1.4).** Join every pair of beats with "but" or "therefore"; where
  "and then" fits, rewrite so the first causes or complicates the second. The
  shape: opening image, catalyst, two or three attempts that each fail
  differently and cost more, a low point, the choice, the final image.
- **Scenes (1.5).** A scene's `change` holds its goal, obstacle and outcome as
  action the camera sees, and the value it ends on, the opposite of where it
  began: "Maya grabs for the kite, but the wind drags it onto the roof; she
  climbs out and frees it, tearing the sail (hope to loss)." The outcome is
  usually a setback or a win at a cost; the decision it forces is the next
  scene's goal, and its end state is the next scene's start state.
- **Setup and payoff.** Show earlier everything the climax uses; pay off every
  plant or cut it. A motif appears three times: introduced, complicated,
  transformed. The final image mirrors the opening one: the same subject and
  composition, changed.
- **Show it.** Write photographable action, never inner states: "she drops the
  key", not "she realises". The film reads with the sound off: narration
  carries only the abstract (a memory, a time jump), never the turn or its
  cause, and never says what the picture shows.
- **What a shot can show.** One clear physical action in about 5 s, by at most
  two characters, with no fine hand work or readable text; a cause and its
  effect are two shots. An action that runs on in one place is one take.

## Check the story before showing it

At every pace and in every review mode, check the story before any piece is
written `approved` or `autoApproved`, and before the treatment is shown or
locked: drafting all six at once, check the six drafts; walked through, check
each piece on the questions it can answer before showing it, then all six
before assembling. Answer each question yes or no against the drafts as a
critic who sees nothing else. When you can start a subagent, give the check of
all six to one, with the pieces and this list, so it runs in a fresh context.

A narrative answers all 13. Another film type, or a shape the user stated (a
loop, a vignette, a mood piece), answers only 12. Under 45 s, 5 is a yes with
one attempt. Every answer must be yes.

1. The logline is one sentence with the protagonist, goal, obstacle and stakes.
2. Exactly one protagonist, whose concrete want is visible in the first 15% of the runtime.
3. Every adjacent pair of beats joins with "but" or "therefore", never "and then".
4. Every scene has a goal, a conflict and an outcome, and ends on a different value than it began.

The creative preferences' _AI video model_ line outranks [the default video model](../SKILL.md) and
this section's models: when it says to confirm, then just before submitting the first paid batch (after any cost approval it needs, or when it needs none), name the model you will use and ask if they want another (once per conversation; keep the answer);
when it names a model, use that family's endpoint for the task (its page under
[models](models/)). Only when it is absent or Agent decides do the defaults apply.

Before the first paid Voyager take, follow [paid generation](craft/paid-generation.md):
check the batch with `voyager models estimate` (cost and credits), fresh for each
batch, and ask first above the spend limit in `<voyager_creative_preferences>`. Once the user approves a batch,
submit every clip in it before waiting on any (a CONTINUE run's next segments
wait for the take they continue, in [waves](continuity.md#multi-shot-practice)),
never one as a trial, unless they asked to see one first. Pass
JSON through a quoted heredoc to preserve literal prompt text:

```sh
voyager models run --input - --json <<'JSON'
{
  "model": "minimax/h3-max/text-to-video",
  "input": {
    "prompt": "A friendly cat stretches in warm sunlight, gentle camera movement",
    "duration": 5,
    "resolution": "768P",
    "aspect_ratio": "16:9",
    "prompt_expansion_mode": "balanced"

```

replace `aspect_ratio` with `image_url: {"$file":"reference.png"}`, and describe the

Pass a short top-level `title` naming the idea (`"title": "Hero shot"`) and reuse it for
retakes of that idea, so its takes share a file name (`hero-shot-take-2.mp4`). Before any

When the delivery needs 1080P, generate at 1080P rather than scaling 768P up ([routes](models/minimax-h3.md#fal-fields)). AI shots cut into the user's footage match its resolution and look.

take and check it against the script. A longer script, a chosen or cloned voice, or one
presenter reused across ads: voice the script first ([voiceover](../../voiceover/SKILL.md)),

# Iterate on a take

Use for any shot or still that goes past its first take. Hold everything but the change.

## Keep a ledger

From the second take of anything, keep a notes file in the project
(`notes/<title>-takes.md`; in a produced film, the shot's entry in
`film/GENERATION.md`) with:

- the base prompt, and the inputs by path (first, last and reference images);
- the locked parameters (below);
- every correction the user has made, verbatim, with its round;
- each take: job ID, file, what changed from the take before, and kept or
  rejected with the reason.

Before submitting a retake, check its prompt and inputs against every ledger line,
not only the latest note. A retake that satisfies the new note by undoing an older
one fails.

## Rebuild the prompt, never patch it

Write each retake's prompt fresh from the shot's spec and the ledger: what the shot
must show, then each correction folded in as the wanted state. Never append a fix
to the last prompt.
Keep it near its first length; when a correction makes a clause redundant, drop
the clause.

## Start from the approved inputs

- Every retake starts from the original approved stills and references, never
  from a rejected take, a frame of one, or a still regenerated from a take.
- Animate exactly the version the user approved. When stills went through
  several versions, the ledger names the approved file.
- Don't grade, recolour or re-shoot an approved still between approval and
  animation. A look change creates a new still.

## Lock everything but the change

Keep the model, endpoint, resolution, duration, aspect ratio and inputs fixed
across takes of one stage (a draft, or the finish), apart from the one change
a retake makes (below). On MiniMax H3, keep `prompt_expansion_mode` the same; `balanced` and
`quality` rewrite the prompt differently each take, and `disabled` keeps your
words as written ([MiniMax H3](models/minimax-h3.md#prompt-expansion-decides-how-much-structure-you-write)).

Change one thing per retake: the prompt, an input or a parameter.

A retake is a new sample. A `seed` doesn't make it repeatable unless the model's
page says the seed works: Seedance 2.5 image-to-video ignores one, and its
reference-to-video takes on one seed are no more alike than unseeded ones. Judge
a change on two or more takes before calling it fixed or regressed.

## Add only what the user asked for

Don't introduce elements the brief didn't ask for: weather, props, a coloured
accessory, a named film stock or cinematographer, a second lens. An element you added that draws a
complaint comes out of the prompt and the stills entirely, not toned down, and the
ledger records it so no later round brings it back. Never describe an unwanted
thing positively ("one woman holding a red umbrella", drizzle) to limit it.

Write people and crowds at the level the user specified. When they say a group
looks wrong, apply their correction as given; don't swing to an exhaustive
checklist or to its opposite.

## Motion verbs belong to the camera

Speed words leak to everything in frame: "the camera races low over the crowd"
makes the crowd race too. Give the camera its move, then the subject
its own pace in a separate sentence: "The camera glides low over the
square. The people below walk at an ordinary, unhurried pace."

## Keep what the user liked

When a long take has a part the user approved and a part they didn't, don't
re-roll the whole move and hope the good part comes back. When the approved part
opens the move, keep it as the first segment and extend from it, retaking only
what follows ([build a long take](film/cinematography.md#build-a-long-take-from-segments)).
Don't pin a middle frame to hold it: that moves the break to the join. Keep the
geography anchor sentence in every retake's prompt.

## Compare each take with the last

Review a retake against the take it replaces, frame by frame at the same
timestamps, and against every ledger line: say what improved and what regressed.
A take that regresses something the user had accepted fails, whatever it fixes.
Run the [AI-artifact pass](review.md#ai-artifact-pass) on every take.

behavior. Separate voice samples from visual references only when the endpoint
supports it; muting a reference is an experiment, not a guaranteed voice-preservation fix.

voiceover; preserve the brief or explain the limitation.

## Repair the right layer

Diagnose policy, schema and transport errors using [production continuity](production-continuity.md).

for scene-local context, duration tradeoffs and approved-state handoffs.
